q: who is considered the father of conceptual art
a: Marcel Duchamp is widely considered the father of conceptual art. A French artist active in the early 20th century, Duchamp challenged traditional notions of what art could be by introducing the concept of the 'readymade' — ordinary manufactured objects that he selected and designated as art. His most famous readymade, 'Fountain' (1917), was a porcelain urinal that he signed with the pseudonym 'R. Mutt' and submitted to an exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists. This work is considered a watershed moment in art history because it shifted the focus from craftsmanship and aesthetics to the artist's idea and intention. Duchamp argued that art is not defined by the skill or technique used to create it, but by the concept behind it. His work laid the foundation for the conceptual art movement that emerged in the 1960s and 1970s, when artists like Joseph Kosuth ('One and Three Chairs'), Sol LeWitt, John Baldessari, and Yoko Ono explicitly prioritized ideas over visual form. Conceptual art asserts that the idea or concept is the most important aspect of the work, and that the finished product is secondary. Duchamp's influence extends beyond conceptual art to movements including Dada, Surrealism, and postmodernism.
